claims.claim: In the National Park Service parks API, Meridian Hill Park is not a standalone park. A search of all 36 NPS units listed for Washington, DC returned no unit named Meridian Hill.
claims.title: findParks (stateCode=DC, limit=50); findParks (q=Meridian Hill)
claims.qualification: Describes how the API represents the park, not its legal status. The q=Meridian Hill search is fuzzy and returned 57 unrelated parks.

claims.claim: The National Park Service represents Meridian Hill Park through Rock Creek Park (park code rocr). Its only Meridian Hill event appears under Rock Creek Park and directs visitors to the Rock Creek Park website.
claims.title: getEvents (parkCode=rocr, q=Meridian)

claims.claim: Rock Creek Park is described by NPS as a 1,754-acre city park authorized in 1890, the third national park designated by the federal government.
claims.title: getParkDetails (parkCode=rocr)
claims.qualification: Quoted from NPS self-description.

claims.claim: Rock Creek Park also administers 99 separate neighborhood small sites. Meridian Hill Park is governed as one of these sites rather than as its own park.
claims.title: getParkDetails (parkCode=rocr), directionsInfo
claims.qualification: The first sentence is quoted from the API. The second sentence combines it with the NPS statement that Meridian Hill is part of Rock Creek Park (nps-web-05). The API does not list the 99 sites by name.

claims.claim: An NPS ranger program scheduled for 17 October 2026, "Mobilizing Memories at Meridian Hill," describes the site as "Meridian Hill Park, colloquially referred to as Malcolm X Park" and as a "First Amendment space." It explores "who we choose to memorialize and why."
claims.title: getEvents (parkCode=rocr, q=Malcolm X)
claims.qualification: The event is tagged 'Freedom 250'. It is a scheduled event and may be cancelled for weather.

claims.claim: On 29 September 2026, the three active Rock Creek Park alerts concerned Waterside Drive, the Nature Center, and Fort Totten. None named Meridian Hill Park.
claims.title: getAlerts (parkCode=rocr)
claims.qualification: Snapshot only. Alerts change. The site does not fetch live alerts.

claims.claim: Rock Creek Park's NPS topic list includes 'Social Movements', 'Music', 'Plantations' and 'Monuments and Memorials'.
claims.title: getParkDetails (parkCode=rocr), topics
claims.qualification: These topics describe the whole Rock Creek Park unit, not Meridian Hill specifically.

claims.claim: The name comes from a mansion. In 1819 a mansion called 'Meridian Hill' was built on the grounds because it stood on the exact longitude of the original District of Columbia milestone marker.
claims.source: NPS, Meridian Hill Park history page
claims.organization: National Park Service, Rock Creek Park
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park
claims.qualification: NPS names the builder as John Porter. Other accounts attribute the house to Commodore David Porter. The discrepancy is preserved rather than resolved.

claims.claim: The milestone marker was set down on 15 April 1791 at Jones Point, Virginia, by Major Andrew Ellicott, assisted by Benjamin Banneker, an African American astronomer and mathematician.
claims.source: NPS, Meridian Hill Park history page
claims.organization: National Park Service, Rock Creek Park
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park

claims.claim: John Quincy Adams moved to the mansion when he left the White House in 1829. During the Civil War, Union troops encamped on the grounds.
claims.source: NPS, Meridian Hill Park history page
claims.organization: National Park Service, Rock Creek Park
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park

claims.claim: In 1910 the United States government purchased the grounds. In 1914 the Department of the Interior hired landscape architect George Burnap, whose plans were later revised by Horace Peaslee. Construction began in 1914 and the park reached full formal status in 1936. The grounds were transferred to the National Park Service in 1933.
claims.source: NPS, Meridian Hill Park history page
claims.organization: National Park Service, Rock Creek Park
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park
claims.qualification: The Cultural Landscape Foundation dates the design and construction to 1912 to 1936. NPS gives 1914 as the start of construction.

claims.claim: NPS describes Meridian Hill Park as 'a part of Rock Creek Park' at 16th and W Streets NW. It lists walking dogs, yoga, dancing, pickup soccer and drumming at a drum circle as things visitors do there.
claims.title: Discover Meridian Hill Park
claims.qualification: Page last updated 12 November 2024.

claims.claim: The park holds a Dante Memorial, one of its earliest works; the James Buchanan Memorial, dedicated in 1930; a Joan of Arc statue, which NPS calls the only female equestrian statue in Washington; 'Serenity' by José Clará, honoring William Henry Schuetze; and the Noyes Armillary Sphere, which was vandalized and removed.
claims.title: Discover Meridian Hill Park

claims.claim: An NPS information panel states: 'Since 1969, the park has unofficially been called "Malcolm X Park" by the local community. As the site of the memorial to President Buchanan, Meridian Hill Park cannot officially be named for another person.'
claims.title: Information Panel: A Gathering Place for Washingtonians (James Buchanan)
claims.qualification: The explanation of why the name cannot be official is the NPS's own statement.

claims.claim: NPS states that since the park opened in 1936, Washingtonians from the surrounding neighborhoods have gathered there for performances, community events and political protest. From 1941 to 1944, summer Starlight Concerts drew crowds to the cascades and reflecting pool.
claims.title: Information Panel: A Gathering Place for Washingtonians (James Buchanan)

claims.claim: After the 1968 assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., the park hosted the opening of the 'Summer in the Parks' concert series. NPS reports that 20,000 people attended the opening performance, which featured Pearl Bailey.
claims.title: Information Panel: A Gathering Place for Washingtonians (James Buchanan)
claims.qualification: The attendance figure is as reported by NPS.

claims.claim: In December 2020, NPS announced a rehabilitation of the lower level. It covered damaged historic walls, walkways and stairs, an accessible route from 16th Street, restoration of the pleached allée framing the Washington Monument view, and storm drains. The cascading fountain was excluded and deferred to a future project pending funding.
claims.organization: National Park Service, Rock Creek Park
claims.title: Rehabilitation Planned for Lower Level of Meridian Hill Park
claims.qualification: Release dated 9 December 2020. It projected completion in summer 2022.

claims.claim: An NPS record of determination, last updated 3 February 2026, closed the lower level through 30 September 2026 and two upper-level grass panels from 23 March to 4 September 2026. The stated purpose was safe rehabilitation of the cascading fountain and water features and restoration of the grass panels. The authority cited was 36 CFR 1.5(a) and 1.7.
claims.organization: National Park Service, Rock Creek Park
claims.title: Record of Determination for a Partial and Temporary Closure of a Portion of Certain Federal Parkland at Meridian Hill Park for Human Health and Safety
claims.qualification: The document does not mention the drum circle, First Amendment activity, or any task force.

claims.claim: The park covers twelve acres. Its 900-foot flat upper terrace, with a central grass mall, side promenades and a linden allée, is French in style. The lower level is Italianate. A central cascade flows through thirteen graduated basins into a large reflecting pool.
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park

claims.claim: Ferruccio Vitale was the chief designer of the planting plan. John Joseph Earley, John L. Paolano and George E. Creed are also credited. The cascade drew on the fountains of the Villa Aldobrandini at Frascati.
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park

claims.claim: Mary Foote Henderson, wife of Missouri Senator John Henderson, promoted the neighborhood as a Beaux-Arts cultural center for Washington. She bought land, commissioned buildings, and lobbied Congress for the park.
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park

claims.claim: Meridian Hill Park became a National Historic Landmark in 1994.
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park
claims.qualification: Industry sources (concreteproducts.com, via search result) add that it was the first NHL in the designed landscape category. That detail was not verified at a primary source.

claims.claim: The Cultural Landscape Foundation describes the park as a 'site of racial protest in the 1970s' that was 'unofficially renamed Malcolm X Park.'
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park
claims.qualification: TCLF says 1970s while NPS dates the name to 1969. The two are shown side by side.

claims.claim: John Joseph Earley developed an exposed-aggregate concrete technique. Pebbles sorted by color and size were set into concrete and the surface scraped as it cured to expose the stone. His cascade at Meridian Hill was completed in 1936.
claims.title: John Joseph Earley; Cascading Waterfall
claims.qualification: Tertiary source read through a search summary. The claim that pebbles came from the Potomac riverbed is omitted pending verification.

claims.claim: DCist reported in 2018 that a leak in cast-iron piping beneath the cascade led NPS to replace about 90 linear feet of pipe. As of 2016, the cascades consumed half the maintenance budget for the park's division. Rock Creek Park faced a deferred maintenance backlog of about $70 million.
claims.title: Why Don't The Fountains At Meridian Hill Park Work?
claims.qualification: Journalism from 2018. The figures reflect that year.

claims.claim: The cascading fountain resumed operation in spring 2026 after about seven years dry. On 2 July 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth held a ceremony at the fountain honoring National Guard members supporting the administration's D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force, created by a March 2025 executive order.
claims.title: Hegseth praises National Guard at restored Meridian Hill Park fountain
claims.qualification: Hegseth's crime-reduction claim is quoted in the article and is not independently verified here. The article quotes no community reaction.

claims.claim: AFP reported in May 2026 that park users feared the beautification drive could erase the park's history as a Black protest and gathering space. A street vendor asked where people could go to express themselves if the park closed. An organizer with the Keep Malcolm X Open Coalition said: 'You don't make a city safe and beautiful by excluding its people!'
claims.title: Fans of historic DC park wary of Trump plan to beautify city
claims.qualification: Dated 19 May 2026. Quotes are attributed by AFP. The coalition's concern about signage removal is reported as a worry, not an event.

claims.claim: AFP reported in 2026 that the weekly drum circle is a decades-long tradition celebrating Black liberation, and that the drum circle area was not yet complete after the fountain reopened.
claims.title: Fans of historic DC park wary of Trump plan to beautify city

claims.claim: Drumming in the park is widely reported to have begun in 1965 as a memorial to Malcolm X after his assassination. Some accounts link it to his birthday, 19 May.
claims.source: Search summary of AFRO, AFP and student press
claims.title: Tradition of drumming in D.C. park going strong after 4 decades (AFRO); AFP 2026
claims.qualification: Oral tradition, repeated by journalism. No primary document from 1965 was located. The AFRO page returned 403 and was not read directly.

claims.claim: One account says drumming dates to the late 1960s and that a formal group was founded in 1975 by a drummer known as Doc Powell.
claims.title: Tradition of drumming in D.C. park going strong after 4 decades
claims.qualification: Read only through a search summary. It conflicts in part with the 1965 origin account. Both are shown.

claims.claim: The uprising after King's assassination lasted from 4 to 8 April 1968. It began near 14th and U Streets NW and spread along 14th Street, U Street, 7th Street, H Street NE and downtown. More than 1,200 fires were reported. 13 people died, about 1,000 were injured and more than 6,100 were arrested. About 6,000 federal and National Guard troops were deployed by the evening of 5 April.
claims.title: 1968 Washington, D.C., riots
claims.qualification: Tertiary source. Figures vary across accounts. See the DC History Center article by Kenneth Schaffer in further reading.

claims.claim: By the 1980s the park had a reputation for crime and drug dealing. Around 1990, residents and community organizations formed the Friends of Meridian Hill, credited to Josephine Butler and others. They ran unarmed, orange-hatted park patrols and received a Partnership Leadership Award from President Clinton in 1994.
claims.source: Project for Public Spaces and Wikipedia, via search summary
claims.title: Neighborhood Reclaims Meridian Hill Park in Washington, DC
claims.qualification: A claim that crime fell by over 95% is omitted as unverified advocacy data. The 'crack park' label is attributed to the Washington Post and was not verified.

claims.claim: The land passed through subdivision after the war. In 1867 the Porter estate was subdivided. From 1887 John and Mary Foote Henderson bought many lots and built a castle-like residence on 16th Street known as 'Boundary Castle'. With architect George Oakley Totten Jr., Mary Henderson developed embassies and mansions along 15th and 16th Streets.
claims.source: Wikipedia, via WebFetch and search summary
claims.title: Meridian Hill; Mary Foote Henderson; Henderson Castle
claims.qualification: Tertiary source.

claims.claim: Accounts report that after the Civil War a working-class, mostly African American community developed on subdivided land nearby, including Wayland Seminary (from 1865), which trained Black clergy and teachers before moving to Richmond in 1899. The same accounts state that around 1912 residents were forced out and houses razed to make way for the park.
claims.title: Meridian Hill (search result summary)
claims.qualification: Displacement is reported but was not confirmed at a primary source during this research. A direct read of the Wikipedia article did not show the passage. A cited Meridian International Center essay, 'Displacement and Development on Meridian Hill', redirected and could not be read. This needs archival verification, for example through land records and the Evening Star.

claims.claim: Meridian Hill is often considered part of the larger neighborhoods of Adams Morgan and Columbia Heights, and sits between them.
claims.title: Meridian Hill
claims.qualification: Neighborhood boundaries in DC are informal and contested.

claims.claim: Search results citing the Society of Architectural Historians state that in the late 1960s the park hosted rallies by African Americans, including protests against urban renewal plans targeting Shaw. They also state that by 1969 Angela Davis and others in the Black Power movement called it Malcolm X Park.
claims.title: Meridian Hill Park (SAH Archipedia)
claims.qualification: The page returned 403 and was not read directly.

claims.claim: Every Data.gov MCP tool (package_search, package_show, group_list, tag_list) returned HTTP 404 on 29 September 2026. The legacy CKAN endpoint at catalog.data.gov/api/3 also returned 404 when called directly.
claims.title: package_search, package_show, group_list, tag_list
claims.qualification: The MCP server appears to target a retired API. Dataset records below come from Data.gov's current public JSON search endpoint, catalog.data.gov/search. They were retrieved by direct HTTP request, not through MCP.

claims.claim: Data.gov lists ten federal and District datasets that bear on the park's context: NPS boundaries and vegetation for Rock Creek Park, the National Register of Historic Places, DC historic districts, EPA park proximity, DC parks, 1950 census tracts, Metro stations and tree canopy.
claims.title: catalog.data.gov/search (see research/datagov_datasets.json)
claims.mcpTool: direct HTTP request to catalog.data.gov/search (Data.gov MCP failed)
claims.qualification: The datasets are listed for context and future analysis. None was downloaded or analyzed for this exhibition, and no statistics are derived from them.

gaps: No documentation of the workers who built the park (1914 to 1936) was located. Their names, wages, race and working conditions are unknown to this research.
The displacement of residents around 1912 is reported but not verified at a primary source.
The origin of the drum circle rests on oral tradition and later journalism.
No archival photographs are reproduced. Drawings in the exhibition are schematic and not to scale.
No demographic statistics are shown, because none of the Data.gov datasets were analyzed.
